passages.where: In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus quotes the seventh commandment and then follows adultery back to the look that desires. The look he means is not a passing glance but a look aimed at having someone, and his words join the command against adultery to the command against coveting a neighbor's wife. He is naming where the sin starts so that it can be stopped there; temptation itself is not sin, and Jesus was tempted too.

Job ends his defense with a long oath of innocence, and the first thing he swears to is about his eyes. He had made a covenant with them before any temptation came. He does not claim to be sinless; he claims to have decided in advance where he would not look, because God sees his ways and counts his steps.

It is the season when kings go to war, and David has stayed home. In an idle evening on the palace roof he sees a woman bathing, sends for her, and takes her. The narrator gives every verb of action to David and holds the king, not Bathsheba, accountable. The sin began with a look in an empty hour, and in the rest of the chapter it hides itself under worse ones.

A father teaches his son to rejoice in the wife of his youth, using the picture of a family's own well, and then warns him away from the stranger. The reason he gives is not only that God sees every path. It is that a man's own sins become the cords that tie him up. Proverbs knows that the thing first chosen can end by holding the one who chose it.

Some in Corinth said that what the body did did not matter to the spirit. Paul answers that the body belongs to the Lord, is a temple of the Holy Spirit, and will be raised. His command is to flee, and his reason is a purchase: you are not your own, you were bought at a price. Just before this he reminds them that some of them had lived this way and had been washed.

Paul tells believers who were once darkness to live as children of light. What is done in secret is shameful even to speak of, he says, but whatever the light exposes becomes visible, and what is lit up becomes light. The way out of the dark in this passage is not more hiding but being seen.

David prays after Nathan has confronted him over Bathsheba. He asks to be washed and made whiter than snow, and then for something only God can do: a clean heart created in him and a right spirit renewed. He does not promise to fix himself; he asks to be made new.

John says that God is light and that walking with him means walking in the light, which includes telling the truth about our sin. Those who say they have no sin deceive themselves. Those who confess find God faithful and just to forgive and to cleanse, and John says this to believers, who keep coming back to it.

James closes his letter with prayer for every condition: the suffering, the cheerful, the sick. Then he widens it to the whole church: confess your sins to each other and pray for each other, so that you may be healed. Confession here is not only to God in private; it is spoken to another believer, who then prays.

Paul gives Titus instructions for every kind of person in the church and grounds them all in one thing: the grace of God has appeared in Christ. That grace does not only forgive; it instructs, training people to say no to worldly passions and to live self-controlled lives. The strength to change is taught by grace, not earned before it.

Hebrews calls Jesus a high priest who is able to sympathize with our weaknesses, because he was tempted in every way that we are, yet without sin. So the reader is told to come to the throne of grace with confidence, to receive mercy and find help at the moment it is needed. The one who hears the confession knows what temptation is.

misread.taken: Paul's words about doing the evil he does not want are quoted as if they settled the matter: this is simply what Christians are like, so there is no point fighting. Others read the same verse the opposite way, as proof that anyone who keeps failing was never a believer at all.
misread.says: Christians differ on who the “I” of these verses is: Paul as a believer, a person under the law without the Spirit, or Paul speaking for someone else. The site's note on the chapter sets out each reading and does not choose. On every reading the passage is not a resting place. It ends in a cry for rescue that is answered with thanks to God through Jesus Christ, and the next chapter opens with no condemnation and with life in the Spirit. The verse names the struggle honestly. It neither excuses the sin nor declares the one who struggles lost.

whole: If this has hold of you, and especially if shame has turned into thoughts of hurting yourself, please speak to someone today; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, and it has a page for exactly this. Pornography rarely feels like a decision. It follows a pattern many people could draw from memory: a long day, a lonely evening, the phone within reach, then the deleted history, the disgust, and the promise that this was the last time. For many it began young, long before they had words for it, and it is not only men who carry it. A spouse who finds it carries something else, a real betrayal that was not their fault.

Scripture does not treat this as a quirk of wiring or a private matter. Jesus followed adultery back to the look aimed at having someone, and he joined the command against adultery to the command against coveting. Desire itself is not the problem; the same Bible delights in married love and tells a husband to rejoice in the wife of his youth. Pornography takes a person made in God's image and makes them an image to be used, and it trains the one who looks to want people that way. David's fall began on a roof in an idle hour, and it hid itself under worse sins. Proverbs says it plainly: a man's own sins become the cords that tie him. That is why willpower alone so often fails. The thing first chosen begins to choose.

The way out runs through the light, not through hating yourself harder. David found that silence wasted him and confession set him free. John promises forgiveness to those who confess, and James tells believers to confess to each other and pray for each other, so that they may be healed. In practice that means telling one person the truth, a pastor, a mature friend, a counselor, or a group that helps people with this. It means doing what Job did and deciding in advance where you will not look, and putting real distance between yourself and the screen, the hour and the place where you fall. It means coming to Jesus as one who was tempted in every way and did not sin, who meets the struggler with mercy and help at the moment it is needed. Grace in Titus is not only pardon. It is a teacher.

Relapse is not the end of the story, and it is not proof that you were never his. Paul's cry of wretchedness was answered with thanks, and the very next words are no condemnation. But grace that forgives also refuses to leave a person where it found them, and the fight is real. To the Corinthians who had lived this way, Paul could write that they had been washed. That word belongs to the one at one in the morning as surely as to anyone else. For the spouse who found out, trust is rebuilt slowly, by truth told over time, and no one may tell you that your grief is the problem. Christ's call to flee and his gift to wash stand together, and neither is cancelled by the other.
sit: Who is one person you could tell the whole truth to this week, and what keeps you from telling them?

prayer.lead: David tells what hiding did to him and what happened when he stopped. Pray it as your own, and let the last line be the one you lean on.

careLines.text: If you are worn down by failing again and again, or caught in an addiction you cannot break, you are not alone, and you are not beyond help.
Please talk to someone: a doctor, a pastor, a counsellor, or a group that helps people with what you are facing.
Paul's command is to flee, and Christ's gift is to wash.
If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
